items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we will learn how to use the special angle relationships formed when a transversal intersects two parallel lines to find unknown angle measures.

Content:
Suppose a transversal cuts across two parallel lines, creating four acute angles and four obtuse angles, as shown below. Let [MATH: \angle A] be one of the acute angles and [MATH: \angle O] be one of the obtuse angles.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/2c7352ee3c8901b6f49a43f4ac2af34c]

Content:
Suppose that we're told that the measure of an obtuse angle is [MATH: (5z + 28)^\circ.] Let's use this information to write down an expression for the measure of the acute angles.

Content:
Recall from a previous lesson that when a transversal intersects two parallel lines, it creates eight angles in total. The four acute angles are all congruent, and the four obtuse angles are all congruent.

Content:
In our case, the measure of one obtuse angle is [MATH: m\angle O = (5z + 28)^\circ.] Since acute and obtuse angles formed in this configuration are supplementary, their measures sum to [MATH: 180^\circ{:}]

Content:
[MATH: m\angle A + m\angle O = 180^\circ]

Content:
Hence, the measure of each acute angle is

Content:
[MATH: m∠A|= 180^{∘} − m∠O; = 180^{∘} − (5z + 28)^{∘}; = 180^{∘} − (5z)^{∘} − 28^{∘}; = 152^{∘} − (5z)^{∘}; = (152 − 5z)^{∘}.]

sections.normalized_html: A line intersects two parallel lines, forming four acute angles and four obtuse angles. The measure of one of the acute angles is [MATH: (96-5t)^\circ,] and the sum of the measures of one of the obtuse angles and two of the acute angles is [MATH: (k-5t)^\circ.] What is the value of [MATH: k?]
sections.readable_text: A line intersects two parallel lines, forming four acute angles and four obtuse angles. The measure of one of the acute angles is [MATH: (96-5t)^\circ,] and the sum of the measures of one of the obtuse angles and two of the acute angles is [MATH: (k-5t)^\circ.] What is the value of [MATH: k?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
When a transversal intersects two parallel lines, it creates eight angles in total: four acute angles and four obtuse angles. All acute angles are congruent, and all obtuse angles are congruent, as shown below.

Let [MATH: \angle A] be an acute angle and [MATH: \angle O] be an obtuse angle.

In our case, [MATH: m\angle A = (96 - 5t)^\circ.]

We are told that the sum of one obtuse angle and two acute angles is [MATH: (k-5t)^\circ.] Writing as an equation, we have

[MATH: m\angle O + 2m\angle A = (k-5t)^\circ.]

We know that [MATH: \angle A] and [MATH: \angle O] are supplementary. Therefore, the left-hand side of the above equation becomes

[MATH: m∠O + 2m∠A|= m∠O + m∠A_(⏟)_(180^{∘}) + m∠A; = 180^{∘} + (96 − 5t)^{∘}; = 276^{∘} − 5t^{∘}.]

Finally, we can equate this to [MATH: (k-5t)^\circ] and solve for [MATH: k,] as follows:

[MATH: 276^{∘} − 5t^{∘}|= k^{∘} − 5t^{∘}; 276|= k; k|= 276]

Content:
Consider the triangles [MATH: RQP] and [MATH: RED] below, where [MATH: \overline{DE}] and [MATH: \overline{PQ}] are parallel. What's the measure of [MATH: \angle RDE?]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/42c67a736194b6437809ced8fa2504c4]

Content:
Since [MATH: \overline{DE}] is parallel to [MATH: \overline{PQ}] and [MATH: \angle{Q}] is a right angle, [MATH: \angle{R E D}] is also a right angle.

Graphic:

Content:
We consider the triangle [MATH: \triangle{RED}.] In any triangle, the sum of the measures of its interior angles is [MATH: 180^\circ.] Therefore,
[MATH: m\angle{RDE} + m\angle{RED} + m\angle{DR E} = 180^\circ.]

Content:
Taking into account that [MATH: m\angle{RED} = 90^\circ] and [MATH: m\angle{DRE} = m\angle{PRQ} = 42^\circ,] we can determine [MATH: m\angle{RDE}] as follows:
[MATH: m∠RDE + m∠RED + m∠DRE|= 180^{∘}; m∠RDE + 90^{∘} + 42^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; m∠RDE + 132^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; m∠RDE|= 48^{∘}]

sections.normalized_html: In a triangle [MATH: \triangle{ABC},] the angle [MATH: \angle{B}] is a right angle. Point [MATH: M] lies on [MATH: \overline{AC},] and point [MATH: N] lies on [MATH: \overline{BC}] such that [MATH: \overline{MN}] is parallel to [MATH: \overline{AB}.] If [MATH: m\angle{ACB} = 31^\circ,] what is the measure, in degrees, of [MATH: \angle AMN?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We proceed to represent the given information in a diagram.

Since [MATH: \overline{MN}] is parallel to [MATH: \overline{AB}] and [MATH: \angle{B}] is a right angle, [MATH: \angle{C N M}] is also a right angle.

We consider the triangle [MATH: \triangle{CNM}.] In any triangle, the sum of the measures of its interior angles is [MATH: 180^\circ.] Therefore, [MATH: m\angle{CMN} + m\angle{CNM} + m\angle{MCN} = 180^\circ.]

Taking into account that [MATH: m\angle{CNM} = 90^\circ] and [MATH: m\angle{MCN} = m\angle{ACB} = 31^\circ,] we can determine [MATH: m\angle{CMN}] as follows: [MATH: m∠CMN + m∠CNM + m∠MCN|= 180^{∘}; m∠CMN + 90^{∘} + 31^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; m∠CMN + 121^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; m∠CMN|= 59^{∘}]

Now, note that [MATH: \angle{AMN}] and [MATH: \angle{CMN}] form a linear pair, so they are supplementary. This means [MATH: m\angle{AMN} + m\angle{CMN} = 180^\circ.]

Finally, substituting [MATH: m\angle{CMN} = 59^\circ] in the equality above and solving for [MATH: m\angle{AMN},] we obtain [MATH: m∠AMN + m∠CMN|= 180^{∘}; m∠AMN + 59^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; m∠AMN|= 121^{∘}.]

Content:
Now, we will see how drawing a line parallel to one side of a right triangle creates a pair of similar triangles, which we can then use to find the lengths of unknown segments.

Content:
For example, suppose we're given the following description:

Content:
> In right triangle [MATH: LMN,] angle [MATH: M] is the right angle and [MATH: MN = 150.] Point [MATH: P] on side [MATH: \overline{LN}] is connected to point [MATH: Q] on side [MATH: \overline{LM}] such that line segment [MATH: \overline{PQ}] is parallel to side [MATH: \overline{MN}] and [MATH: N P = 4 L P.] What is the length of [MATH: \overline{PQ}?]

Content:
We'll now proceed to draw a diagram from this description and calculate the required side length [MATH: \overline{PQ}.]

Content:
Since [MATH: \triangle LMN] is a right triangle with the right angle at [MATH: M,] and [MATH: \overline{PQ} \parallel \overline{MN}] (where point [MATH: P] lies on side [MATH: \overline{LN}] and point [MATH: Q] lies on side [MATH: \overline{LM}]), the triangles can be represented as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/db77d35f2e58d3fb9937f37c14589df4]

Content:
Please take a moment to ensure you understand why this diagram accurately represents the given description.

Content:
In the triangles [MATH: \triangle LQP] and [MATH: \triangle LMN,] there are two pairs of congruent angles:

Content:
- [MATH: \angle PQL \cong \angle NML] since both are right angles, and
- [MATH: \angle L] is common to both triangles.

Content:
Since two pairs of corresponding angles are congruent, the triangles are similar by the AA similarity criterion. Therefore,
[MATH: \dfrac{PQ}{MN}=\dfrac{LP}{LN}.]

Content:
Since [MATH: NP = 4 LP,] we have that
[MATH: LN|= LP + NP; = LP + 4LP; = 5LP.]

Content:
Therefore, since [MATH: MN=150,] we obtain the following equations that we solve for [MATH: PQ{:}]
[MATH: (PQ)/(MN)|= (LP)/(LN); (PQ)/(150)|= (LP)/(5LP); (PQ)/(150)|= (1)/(5); PQ|= (1)/(5) ⋅ 150; PQ|= 30.]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: PQ = 30] units.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we will learn how to use the special angle relationships formed when a transversal intersects two parallel lines to find unknown angle measures.

Content:
Suppose a transversal cuts across two parallel lines, creating four acute angles and four obtuse angles, as shown below. Let [MATH: \angle A] be one of the acute angles and [MATH: \angle O] be one of the obtuse angles.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/2c7352ee3c8901b6f49a43f4ac2af34c]

Content:
Suppose that we're told that the measure of an obtuse angle is [MATH: (5z + 28)^\circ.] Let's use this information to write down an expression for the measure of the acute angles.

Content:
Recall from a previous lesson that when a transversal intersects two parallel lines, it creates eight angles in total. The four acute angles are all congruent, and the four obtuse angles are all congruent.

Content:
In our case, the measure of one obtuse angle is [MATH: m\angle O = (5z + 28)^\circ.] Since acute and obtuse angles formed in this configuration are supplementary, their measures sum to [MATH: 180^\circ{:}]

Content:
[MATH: m\angle A + m\angle O = 180^\circ]

Content:
Hence, the measure of each acute angle is

Content:
[MATH: m∠A|= 180^{∘} − m∠O; = 180^{∘} − (5z + 28)^{∘}; = 180^{∘} − (5z)^{∘} − 28^{∘}; = 152^{∘} − (5z)^{∘}; = (152 − 5z)^{∘}.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Determining Angles From Descriptions of Parallel Lines and Transversals

Example Prompt:
A line intersects two parallel lines, forming four acute angles and four obtuse angles. The measure of one of the acute angles is [MATH: (96-5t)^\circ,] and the sum of the measures of one of the obtuse angles and two of the acute angles is [MATH: (k-5t)^\circ.] What is the value of [MATH: k?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
When a transversal intersects two parallel lines, it creates eight angles in total: four acute angles and four obtuse angles. All acute angles are congruent, and all obtuse angles are congruent, as shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/b3d7bc6f4cea0a6f3152fa1190e54a29]

Let [MATH: \angle A] be an acute angle and [MATH: \angle O] be an obtuse angle.

In our case,
[MATH: m\angle A = (96 - 5t)^\circ.]

We are told that the sum of one obtuse angle and two acute angles is [MATH: (k-5t)^\circ.] Writing as an equation, we have

[MATH: m\angle O + 2m\angle A = (k-5t)^\circ.]

We know that [MATH: \angle A] and [MATH: \angle O] are supplementary. Therefore, the left-hand side of the above equation becomes

[MATH: m∠O + 2m∠A|= m∠O + m∠A_(⏟)_(180^{∘}) + m∠A; = 180^{∘} + (96 − 5t)^{∘}; = 276^{∘} − 5t^{∘}.]

Finally, we can equate this to [MATH: (k-5t)^\circ] and solve for [MATH: k,] as follows:

[MATH: 276^{∘} − 5t^{∘}|= k^{∘} − 5t^{∘}; 276|= k; k|= 276]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: Parallel Lines in Embedded Triangles

Content:
Now, we will learn how parallel lines inside a triangle create corresponding and alternate interior angles that help us find unknown angle measures.

Content:
Consider the triangles [MATH: RQP] and [MATH: RED] below, where [MATH: \overline{DE}] and [MATH: \overline{PQ}] are parallel. What's the measure of [MATH: \angle RDE?]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/42c67a736194b6437809ced8fa2504c4]

Content:
Since [MATH: \overline{DE}] is parallel to [MATH: \overline{PQ}] and [MATH: \angle{Q}] is a right angle, [MATH: \angle{R E D}] is also a right angle.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4341ad8c70abc4d98b92436063e8f9c5]

Content:
We consider the triangle [MATH: \triangle{RED}.] In any triangle, the sum of the measures of its interior angles is [MATH: 180^\circ.] Therefore,
[MATH: m\angle{RDE} + m\angle{RED} + m\angle{DR E} = 180^\circ.]

Content:
Taking into account that [MATH: m\angle{RED} = 90^\circ] and [MATH: m\angle{DRE} = m\angle{PRQ} = 42^\circ,] we can determine [MATH: m\angle{RDE}] as follows:
[MATH: m∠RDE + m∠RED + m∠DRE|= 180^{∘}; m∠RDE + 90^{∘} + 42^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; m∠RDE + 132^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; m∠RDE|= 48^{∘}]

Content:
We often need to solve similar problems by drawing a diagram from a description that's given to us. In such cases, we need to read the information we're given carefully and draw a diagram that accurately represents the description.

Item 6 — Example: Determining Angles From Descriptions of Embedded Right Triangles

Example Prompt:
In a triangle [MATH: \triangle{ABC},] the angle [MATH: \angle{B}] is a right angle. Point [MATH: M] lies on [MATH: \overline{AC},] and point [MATH: N] lies on [MATH: \overline{BC}] such that [MATH: \overline{MN}] is parallel to [MATH: \overline{AB}.] If [MATH: m\angle{ACB} = 31^\circ,] what is the measure, in degrees, of [MATH: \angle AMN?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We proceed to represent the given information in a diagram.

[IMG: /graphics/24332e3f4ddc40f210a884e0bc9dec1c]

Since [MATH: \overline{MN}] is parallel to [MATH: \overline{AB}] and [MATH: \angle{B}] is a right angle, [MATH: \angle{C N M}] is also a right angle.

We consider the triangle [MATH: \triangle{CNM}.] In any triangle, the sum of the measures of its interior angles is [MATH: 180^\circ.] Therefore,
[MATH: m\angle{CMN} + m\angle{CNM} + m\angle{MCN} = 180^\circ.]

Taking into account that [MATH: m\angle{CNM} = 90^\circ] and [MATH: m\angle{MCN} = m\angle{ACB} = 31^\circ,] we can determine [MATH: m\angle{CMN}] as follows:
[MATH: m∠CMN + m∠CNM + m∠MCN|= 180^{∘}; m∠CMN + 90^{∘} + 31^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; m∠CMN + 121^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; m∠CMN|= 59^{∘}]

Now, note that [MATH: \angle{AMN}] and [MATH: \angle{CMN}] form a linear pair, so they are supplementary. This means
[MATH: m\angle{AMN} + m\angle{CMN} = 180^\circ.]

Finally, substituting [MATH: m\angle{CMN} = 59^\circ] in the equality above and solving for [MATH: m\angle{AMN},] we obtain
[MATH: m∠AMN + m∠CMN|= 180^{∘}; m∠AMN + 59^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; m∠AMN|= 121^{∘}.]
